20. For where two or three are assembled in my name. This promise is more extensive than the former; for the Lord declares that he will be present,
wherever two or three are met together in his name, to guide them by his counsel, (Psalm 73:24,)
and to conduct to a prosperous result whatever they shall undertake. There is therefore no reason to doubt that those who give themselves up to his direction will derive most desirable advantage from his presence. And since it is an invaluable blessing to have Christ for our director in all our affairs, to bless our deliberations and their results; and since, on the other hand, nothing can be more miserable than to be deprived of his grace, this promise ought to add no small excitement to us to unite with each other in piety and holiness.
“A nous lier les uns avec les autres en toute sainctete et crainte de Dieu;” — “to link ourselves with each other in all holiness and fear of God.”
For whoever either disregards the holy assemblies, or separates himself from brethren, and takes little interest in the cultivation of unity, by this alone makes it evident that he sets no value on the presence of Christ.
But we must take care, first of all, that those who are desirous to have Christ present with them shall assemble in his name; and we must likewise understand what is the meaning of this expression; for we perceive how ungodly men falsely and impudently, as well as wickedly, cover their conspiracies with his sacred name. If therefore we do not wish to expose Christ to their ridicule, and at the same time to overturn what he has here promised, we must know first of all what is meant by this phrase. It means that those who are assembled together, laying aside every thing that hinders them from approaching to Christ, shall sincerely raise their desires to him, shall yield obedience to his word, and allow themselves to be governed by the Spirit. Where this simplicity prevails, there is no reason to fear that Christ will not make it manifest that it was not in vain for the assembly to meet in his name
In this is displayed the gross ignorance of the Papists, who exclaim that Councils could not err, and that all ought to abide by their decisions, because, as often as two or three are assembled in the name of Christ, he is in the midst of them But we ought first of all to inquire whether those persons, as to whose faith, and doctrine, and dispositions, we are in doubt, were assembled in the name of Christ. When the Papists leave out or perplex this matter, who does not see that they dexteroasly confound the distinction between holy and profane assemblies, so that the power of doing any thing is taken from the Church and conveyed to the sworn enemies of Christ? Let us therefore know that none but the pious worshippers of God, who sincerely seek Christ, are encouraged to entertain the confident hope that he will never leave them. Disregarding the bastard and abortive Councils, which out of their own head have woven a web, let Christ alone, with the doctrine of his Gospel, be always exalted amongst us.

entries.55a57d1fc938f23a2fb2b6f6b26513bfdae5bce7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.21" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.18.21" sID="gen100694" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.18.21">Matthew 18:21</reference>. </hi><hi type="italic">Lord, how often shall my brother offend against me?</hi> Peter made this objection according to the natural feelings and disposition of the flesh. It is natural to all men to wish to be forgiven; and, therefore, if any man does not immediately obtain forgiveness, he complains that he is treated with sternness and cruelty. But those who demand to be treated gently are far from being equally gentle towards others; and therefore, when our Lord exhorted his disciples to meekness, this doubt occurred to Peter: “If we be so strongly disposed to grant forgiveness, what will be the consequence, but that our lenity shall be an inducement to <hi type="italic">offend</hi>?” <note n="571"> <div sID="gen100696" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Incitera les autres a mal faire, et a nous offenser</foreign>;” — “shall induce others to do ill, and to offend us.”<div eID="gen100696" type="x-p"/> </note> He asks, therefore, if it be proper frequently to forgive offenders; for, since the number <hi type="italic">seven </hi>is taken for a large number, the force of the adverb, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἑπτάκις</foreign>) <hi type="italic">seven times</hi>, is the same as if he had said, “How long, Lord, dost thou wish that offenders be received into favor? for it is unreasonable, and by no means advantageous, that they should, in every case, find us willing to be reconciled.” But Christ is so far from yielding to this objection, that he expressly declares that there ought to be no limit to forgiving; <note n="572"> <div sID="gen100697" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais tant s’en faut que Christ ait esgard a ceste objection pour lascher quelque chose de son dire, que mesmes il dit notamment et expressement que sans fin ne terme on doit tousiours pardonner</foreign>;” — “but so far was Christ from paying regard to that objection, to extenuate any thing that he had said, that he even says plainly and expressly, that without end or limit we must always forgive.”<div eID="gen100697" type="x-p"/> </note> for he did not intend to lay down a fixed number, but rather to enjoin us never to become wearied.<div eID="gen100695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100698" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Luke </hi>differs somewhat from <hi type="italic">Matthew</hi>; for he states the command of Christ to be simply, that we should be prepared to <hi type="italic">forgive seven times; </hi>but the meaning is the same, that we ought to be ready and prepared to grant forgiveness not once or twice, but as often as the sinner <hi type="italic">shall repent</hi> There is only this difference between them, that, according to Matthew, our Lord, in reproving Peter for taking too limited a view, employs hyperbolically a larger number, which of itself is sufficient to point out the substance of what is intended. For when Peter asked if he should <hi type="italic">forgive seven times,</hi> it was not because he did not choose to go any farther, but, by presenting the appearance of a great absurdity, to withdraw Christ from his opinion, as I have lately hinted. So then he who shall be prepared to <hi type="italic">forgive seven times</hi> will be willing to be reconciled as far as to the <hi type="italic">seventieth </hi>offense.<div eID="gen100698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100699" type="x-p"/>But the words of Luke give rise to another question; for Christ does not order us to grant <hi type="italic">forgiveness</hi>, till<hi type="italic"> the offender turn </hi>to us and give evidence of <hi type="italic">repentance</hi>. <note n="573"> <div sID="gen100700" type="x-p"/> In the French copy he adds: — “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car il semble par ce moyen qu’il commande aux siens de tenir leur coeur contre les pervers, et leur refuser pardon</foreign>;” — “for it appears in this way that he commands his followers to shut their heart against the obstinate, and to refuse them pardon.”<div eID="gen100700" type="x-p"/> </note> I reply, there are two ways in which offenses are <hi type="italic">forgiven. </hi>If a man shall do me an injury, and I, laying aside the desire of revenge, do not cease to love him, but even repay kindness in place of injury, though I entertain an unfavorable opinion of him, as he deserves, still I am said to<hi type="italic"> forgive him</hi>. For when God commands us to wish well to our enemies, He does not therefore demand that we approve in them what He condemns, but only desires that our minds shall be purified from all hatred. In this kind of pardon, so far are we from having any right to wait till he who has offended shall return of his own accord to be reconciled to us, that we ought to love those who deliberately provoke us, who spurn reconciliation, and add to the load of former offenses. A second kind of <hi type="italic">forgiving </hi>is, when we receive a <hi type="italic">brother </hi>into favor, so as to think favorably respecting him, and to be convinced that the remembrance of his offense is blotted out in the sight of God. And this is what I have formerly remarked, that in this passage Christ does not speak only of injuries which have been done to us, but of every kind of offenses; for he desires that, by our compassion, we shall raise up those who have fallen. <note n="574"> <div sID="gen100701" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Ceux qui sont cheus et ont failli</foreign>;” — “those who are fallen and have transgressed.”<div eID="gen100701" type="x-p"/> </note> This doctrine is very necessary, because naturally almost all of us are peevish beyond measure; and Satan, under the pretense of severity, drives us to cruel rigor, so that wretched men, to whom pardon is refused, are swallowed up by grief and despair.<div eID="gen100699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100702" type="x-p"/>But here another question arises. As soon as a man by words makes profession of <hi type="italic">repentance</hi>, are we bound to believe him? Were this done, we must of necessity go willingly and knowingly into mistake; for where will be discretion, if any man may freely impose on us, even to the hundredth offense? I answer, <hi type="italic">first</hi>, the discourse relates here to daily faults, in which every man, even the best, needs forgiveness. <note n="575"> <div sID="gen100703" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Esquelles les plus parfaits mesmes ont besoin d’estre supportez, et qu’on leur pardonner</foreign>;” — “which even the most perfect need to be borne with and forgiven.”<div eID="gen100703" type="x-p"/> </note> Since, then, amidst such infirmity of the flesh, our road is so slippery, and snares and attacks so numerous what will be the consequence if, at the second or third fall, the hope <hi type="italic">of forgiveness </hi>is cut off? We must add, <hi type="italic">secondly, </hi>that Christ does not deprive believers of the exercise of judgment, so as to yield a foolish readiness of belief to every slight expression, but only desires us to be so candid and merciful, as to stretch out the hand to <hi type="italic">offenders</hi>,<hi type="italic"> </hi>provided there be evidence that they are sincerely dissatisfied with their sins. For repentance is a sacred thing, and therefore needs careful examination; but as soon as the offender gives probable evidence of conversion, Christ desires that he shall be admitted to reconciliation, lest, on being repulsed, he lose courage and fall back.<div eID="gen100702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen100704" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Thirdly</hi>, It must be observed that, when any man, through his light and unsteady behavior, has exposed himself to suspicion, we may grant pardon when he asks it, and yet may do so in such a manner as to watch over his conduct for the future, that our forbearance and meekness, which proceed from the Spirit of Christ, may not become the subject of his ridicule. For we must observe the design of our Lord himself, that we ought, by our gentleness, to assist those who have fallen to rise again. And certainly we ought to imitate the goodness of our heavenly Father, who meets sinners at a distance to invite them to salvation. Besides, as repentance is a wonderful work of the Spirit, and is the creation of the new man, if we despise it, we offer an insult to God himself.<div eID="gen100704" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.21" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100694" osisID="Matt.18.21" type="section"/>
entries.85606d795aa75874fd4fb1751bbe74d09dfa8d9e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.18.23" sID="gen100705" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23. </hi><hi type="italic">The kingdom of heaven is compared.</hi> As it is difficult to bend us to mercy, and as we are quickly seized with weariness, particularly when we have to bear with many faults of brethren, our Lord confirms this doctrine by a most appropriate parable, the substance of which is, that those who will not yield to pardon the faults of brethren judge very ill for themselves, and subject themselves to a very hard and severe law; for they will find God to be equally stern and inexorable towards themselves. There are three parts in which the resemblance mainly consists; for the <hi type="italic">master </hi>is contrasted with the <hi type="italic">servant</hi>, the large sum of money with small or ordinary sums, and extraordinary kindness with extreme cruelty. By attending to these three points, it will be easy to ascertain Christ’s meaning; for what are we, if we are compared with God? And how large is the sum which every one of us owes to God? Lastly, how inconsiderable are the offenses, with which brethren are chargeable towards us, if we take into account our obligation to God? How ill then does that man deserve the compassion of God, who, though oppressed with an immense load, implacably refuses to forgive even the smallest offenses to men like himself? So far as regards the words, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven</hi> here denotes the spiritual condition of the Church; as if Christ had said, that the state of matters between God and men, in regard to the soul and the nature of spiritual life, is the same as between an ordinary or earthly <hi type="italic">master </hi>and his <hi type="italic">servants</hi>, in regard to money and the affairs of the present life.<div eID="gen100706" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100705" osisID="Matt.18.23" type="section"/>
entries.5e421032a743d3c19eb7b08a74cc017639083922: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.18.25" sID="gen100707" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25. </hi><hi type="italic">His master ordered him to be sold.</hi> It would be an idle exercise of ingenuity to examine here every minute clause. For God does not always display severity at first, till, constrained to pray, we implore pardon, but rather meets us with undeserved goodness. But Christ only shows what will become of us, if God shall treat us with the utmost severity; and again, if He shall choose to demand from us what we owe, how necessary it is for us to betake ourselves to prayer, because this is the only refuge that remains for transgressors. We must also attend to the wide difference of the sums; for, since one <hi type="italic">talent </hi>is worth more than <hi type="italic">a hundred pence</hi>, what proportion will <hi type="italic">a hundred pence </hi>bear to <hi type="italic">ten thousand talents?</hi><div eID="gen100708" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100707" osisID="Matt.18.25" type="section"/>
entries.2004ae13828612d6b1566d7311bb27feb2206036: <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Matt.18.31" sID="gen100709" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100710" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31. </hi><hi type="italic">When his fellow-servants saw what was done.</hi> Though we ought not to search for mystery in these words — because they contain nothing but what nature teaches, and what we learn by daily experience — we ought to know that the men who live among us will be so many witnesses against us before God; for it is impossible but that cruelty shall excite in them displeasure and hatred, more especially, since every man is afraid that what he sees done to others will fall upon his own head. As to the clause which immediately follows, it is foolish to inquire how God punishes those sins <note n="576"> <div sID="gen100711" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comment il est possible que Dieu punisse</foreign>;” — “how it is possible for God to punish.”<div eID="gen100711" type="x-p"/> </note> which he has already forgiven; for the simple meaning is this: though he offers mercy to all, yet severe creditors, from whom no forgiveness can be obtained, are unworthy of enjoying it.<div eID="gen100710" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Matt.18.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100709" osisID="Matt.18.31" type="section"/>

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 1.19.) some of them had more extraordinary parts, he Named two of them on this account, <ns0:hi>the Sons of Thunder,</ns0:hi> To others he had shewed a more particular kindness. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> is called the <ns0:hi>beloved Disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, Peter, Iames</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> were taken up to the Mount to see his <ns0:hi>Transfiguration.</ns0:hi> These things might cause some <ns0:hi>E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mulation</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Suspicions,</ns0:hi> they therefore come to our Saviour to be resolved. 1. How slowly do we conceive, and how hardly do we come to understand Spiritual things? we are of the Earth, and we are Earthly. 2. How prone are we to seek great things for our selves? neglecting our higher Spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual, and Eternal concerns? This Text lets us see, that even the best of Men are subject to <ns0:hi>Earthly mindedness, Ambiti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, Emulation,</ns0:hi> and hardly brought truly to understand, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve, and seek the things which are above.                </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 And Jesus called a little child unto him, and set him in the midst of them.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 And said unto them, Verily I say unto you, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 19.14. 1 Cor. 14<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 20.3. 1 Pet. 2.2.</ns0:note> Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:251" />
this little child, the same is greatest in the king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of heaven.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9.35. <ns0:hi>And he sate down, and called the twelve, and said unto them, if any Man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all; and Servant of all. And he took a Child and set him in the midst of them, and when he had taken him in his Arms, he said unto them,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> saith only, <ns0:hi>that he took the Child, and set him by him, Ch.</ns0:hi> 9.47. and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 48. <ns0:hi>and adds, He that is least amongst you all, the same shall be great.</ns0:hi> How easie a thing had it been for our Saviour, had he intended any such <ns0:hi>Primacy</ns0:hi> in the Church, as the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> contend for, to have said, <ns0:hi>Peter shall be the greatest.</ns0:hi> Here was a very fair opportunity for him, if he had pleased, so to have declared his Will, but here is not a Word of such Tendency. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> saith, our Saviour fir<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t <ns0:hi>sate down</ns0:hi> (as the manner of their Teachers was, when they taught, to denote their Authority) 2. <ns0:hi>He called the twelve,</ns0:hi> to let them know, that what he was about to speak, was a grave matter, not of a particular, but universal concern, for them to learn, that they might teach others. He said to them (saith <ns0:hi>Mark) If any Man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and Servant of all, and</ns0:hi> (which <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> adds) <ns0:hi>He that is least amongst you all, the same shall be Great.</ns0:hi> You would know (saith he) who shall be greatest, He that doth not de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire to be first, he who is most remote fro<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>Pride,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bition,</ns0:hi> he that most contemneth the World, and the <ns0:hi>Priori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Superiorities</ns0:hi> of it. The Proud and Ambitious Man, he that seeketh great things for himself, shall be of least e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />steem in my Kingdom, he is really least in Grace, and ought to be of least esteem, and repute amongst Christians, and he will be the last in the Kingdom of Glory. <ns0:hi>Then he calleth to him a little Child,</ns0:hi> the Word doth not always signify a very young Child, here it doth, for, 1. He took him in his Arms (saith <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi>) 2. A <ns0:hi>Young Child</ns0:hi> was the fittest pattern to commend Humility to them. This was an Ancient and usual way of teaching, by Types as it were, or Patterns. See <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 19.10. and 27. 2. He reads this Lecture upon the Child, <ns0:hi>Veri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly except ye be converted, and become as little Children, ye cannot enter into the Kingdom of God. Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little Child,</ns0:hi> &c. The prefixing <ns0:hi>Verily</ns0:hi> adds much to the Authority of this saying. <ns0:hi>Converted here</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> doth not signify the Change or Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />version of a Soul from a <ns0:hi>State of Sin unto God</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> (so the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles were already converted) but the turning of their Souls from a particular Lust or Error, into the opposite right way of Truth, and Holiness; except ye repent of your <ns0:hi>Pride</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ambition,</ns0:hi> ye cannot be saved, the next Words Expound it, <ns0:hi>and become as little Children.</ns0:hi> Not as little Children in all things (which was the <ns0:hi>Anabaptists</ns0:hi> Dream in <ns0:hi>Germany,</ns0:hi> upon which they would run about the Streets, playing with Rattles, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>) but <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. <ns0:hi>Humbling your selves as little Children.</ns0:hi> Little Children know not what Dominion means, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore affect it not, are not Ambitious. 2. They are not gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven to Boast and Glory, and to prefer themselves before others. 3. They are ready to be taught and instructed. 4. They live upon their Fathers Providence, and are not over Sollicitous. 5. They are not Malitious, and Vindicative; <ns0:hi>in Malice</ns0:hi> (saith the Apostle) <ns0:hi>be ye Children.</ns0:hi> The three first are principally here intended. If ye be not thus like little Children, ye will be so far from being greatest in the Kingdom of God, that you will never come there at all. So as this Text teacheth us all, 1. The necessity of Humility in order to Salvation. 2. That even converted Souls have need of a daily <ns0:hi>Conversion,</ns0:hi> Repentance is a Work will never be perfected till we come to dye. 3. How abominable in the Eyes of God <ns0:hi>Ambition</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pride</ns0:hi> in any, especially in Ministers of the Gospel are. 4. That in the Church, the way to be great, is to be humble. 5. That true Humility lyeth in a mean opinion of our selves, <ns0:hi>not minding high things, Condescending to men of low E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />state, not being wise in our own Conceits,</ns0:hi> Rom. 12.16. <ns0:hi>in Honour preferring one another,</ns0:hi> v. 10.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And whoso shall receive one such little child in my name, receiveth me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 But <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mark 9, 42. Luke 17.1, 2.</ns0:note> whoso shall offend one of these little ones, which believe in me, it were better for him that a milstone were hang'd about his neck, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> he were drowned in the depth of the Sea.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath it thus, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9.37. <ns0:hi>whosoever shall receive one of such Children in my Name, receiveth me, and who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever receiveth me, receiveth not me, but him that sent me; then,</ns0:hi> v. 42. he addeth, <ns0:hi>And whosoever shall offend one of these little ones that believe in me, it is better for him that</ns0:hi> a <ns0:hi>Milstone were hang'd about his Neck<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and he were cast into the Sea.</ns0:hi> Our Lord having declared that the little ones before mentioned, shall be greatest in the Kingdom of God, here cometh to shew the care, which he in his Providence will take for them. That their Friends shall be his Friends, and their <ns0:hi>Enemies</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Enemies.</ns0:hi> Whoso receiveth <ns0:hi>such a lit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle Child,</ns0:hi> that is, an humble Christian. In the next <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> it is opened by <ns0:hi>one that believeth in me.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>receiving,</ns0:hi> I conceive is here to be understood the shewing of any favour, or kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness to them, Christ declares that he would take it as don<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to himself. It is much the same with <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 10.40, 41, 42. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> addeth, <ns0:hi>He that receiveth me, receiveth him that sent me.</ns0:hi> The Reason is, because he and his Father are one, and the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> takes any kindness done to Christ, as if it were done to himself, and the Son takes any kindness, or unkind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness done to any humble, believing Soul, as if it were done to himself, see <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 25. from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 34. to the end. <ns0:hi>And whoso shall offend any of these little ones,</ns0:hi> &c, As <ns0:hi>offending</ns0:hi> signifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ieth the <ns0:hi>laying of a Stumbling Block</ns0:hi> before any, so it signifi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth any Motion, or Temptation to them to Sin against God, whether it be by Flattering or Frowning Arguments, tho the latter seemeth rather to be understood here; so by <ns0:hi>offending,</ns0:hi> it signifies the doing of them any harm upon Christs account, because they own him, and make a profe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>sion of his Gospel, which besides that, it is a <ns0:hi>Stumbling Block,</ns0:hi> upon which they fall and suffer as to their Bodies and outward concerns, is also a Stumbling Block to their Souls, such dangers being strong Temptations to Christians, to turn them aside from the right Pathes of Truth, and Holiness. <ns0:hi>It were better for him that a Milstone,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, a stone in such a Mill as Asses were wont to draw, because of the heaviness of it. Some think our Saviour in this Phrase alludeth to some punishment of Notorious Malefactors, in use not amongst the Jews, but some other Nations, by tying a Stone about their Necks, and throwing them into the Sea; but whether it be such an allusion or no, is of no great Moment; the <ns0:hi>Phrase</ns0:hi> signifyeth a cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain Destruction, both in regard of the Weight of the Stone, and the depth of the Sea. He saith, <ns0:hi>It is better that a Milstone,</ns0:hi> &c because of the punishment shall be inflicted on such Persons, beyond this Life.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Woe unto the world, because of offen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 11.19.</ns0:note> For it must needs be that offences come, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 26<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 24.</ns0:note> woe to that man by whom the offence cometh.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Wherefore if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off, and cast <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> from thee, it is better for thee to enter into life, halt, or maimed, rather than having two hands, or two feet, to be cast into everlasting fire.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> from thee, it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes, to be cast into hell fire.<ns0:note place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Offences</ns0:hi> are here meant <ns0:hi>Stumbling Blocks</ns0:hi> to Souls, such Persons or Actions as are to others <ns0:hi>Temptations to Sin.</ns0:hi> The World, saith our Saviour, is full of <ns0:hi>Temptations.</ns0:hi> Temptati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons to Sin are on all Hands, some inticing and persuading Men to that which is Evil, others setting them an Example to it, others alluring them by promises, others by threatnings and punishments driving Men to it as much as in them lyeth; the World will one day find the Evil, and Mischief of it. <ns0:hi>It must be that offences come,</ns0:hi> God hath so ordered it in the Wisdom of his Providence, that he will not restrain the Lusts of all Mens Hearts, but suffer some to walk in their own ways. Men in Power will command those under them, to do what is Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful, fright them by Threatnings, force them (if possible) by Punishments. <ns0:hi>Equals</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Inferiours</ns0:hi> will set examples of Sin, Allure, Intice and perswade. But <ns0:hi>Woe be to those by whom such Offences come.</ns0:hi> Men, saith our Saviour, should be so a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fraid to Sin, as they should rather part with the dearest things they have in the World, if they be as dear as <ns0:hi>Eyes, Hands, Feet,</ns0:hi> rather than Sin, or indure them to be occasions of Sin to them, See <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8, 9. opened in our Notes on <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 5.29. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> hath the same things. <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 9.43<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 44, 45, 46, 47, 48. only with the addition of this saying thrice. <ns0:hi>Where the Worm dyeth not, and the Fire is not quenched.</ns0:hi> Which Phrase doth but denote the Eternity of Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners Misery taken from <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> 66. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones, for I say unto you, that in hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Z<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>c. 13.2.</ns0:note> their Angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour having before declared, how dear believing Souls are unto him, tho their quality, or parts be not like o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers, here he gives the Word a further charge not to <ns0:hi>despise,</ns0:hi> that is, not to <ns0:hi>Contemn</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>neglect</ns0:hi> them, because God the Heavenly Father hath such a care of them, so as he hath gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven <ns0:hi>his Angels a charge over them, Psal.</ns0:hi> 34.7. <ns0:hi>Psal,</ns0:hi> 91.11. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.14. which Angels (saith he) do always behold <ns0:hi>the Face of my Father,</ns0:hi> which is in Heaven, that is, are always Ministring before him, and ready to execute his Will, and pleasure; so as the Argument is not only drawn from the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />decency, and undutifulness, that such <ns0:hi>despising</ns0:hi> must import, but also from the danger of it. <ns0:hi>Your heavenly Father</ns0:hi> so loveth these little ones, that he hath given his Angels a <ns0:hi>special charge</ns0:hi> concerning them, and these Angels being continual<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly in the Lords presence, are ready both to make report how they are used in the World, and likewise having Commission from God, to execute his Vengeance upon those who <ns0:hi>neg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect, despise,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>affront</ns0:hi> those that he hath taken into such a special <ns0:hi>Protection.</ns0:hi> Here is no ground in this Text for t<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eir Notion, who Fancy that every particular Child of God hath his <ns0:hi>proper Angel</ns0:hi> to attend them. Our Saviour doth not say their several; and respective Angels, but <ns0:hi>their Angels,</ns0:hi> and if all the Angels be <ns0:hi>ministring Spirits, for the good of Gods Elect, Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.14. I see no great reason to contend for a par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticular Angel, for every individual amongst them. But be that as <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t will, the Opinion hath no Patronage from this Text.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:251" />11 <ns0:note place="margin">Luk. 19.10,</ns0:note> For the son of man is come to save that which was lost.<ns0:note place="bottom">We find the same in <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 19.10. but applyed upon another occasion. Our Saviour here riseth higher in his Argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, against <ns0:hi>giving Offence to his little Ones.</ns0:hi> All <ns0:hi>Scandal</ns0:hi> tendeth to the Ruin and Destruction of him to whom it is given. <ns0:hi>Scandalum non est nisi malae rei aedificans ad Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hennam,</ns0:hi> saith <ns0:hi>Tertull.</ns0:hi> and a greater than he hath tau<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ht us the same Lesson, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 14, 15. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 8.11. Now (saith our Saviour) <ns0:hi>I am come to save that which was lost,</ns0:hi> you ought therefore to take Care, that you be not the Causes and In<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of any being lost. Or thus, you look upon poor hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble Souls, that believe in me, as mean Contemptible Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLunhyphen" />tures, therefore you think you may despise them: Were not all those whom I came to redeem, in as mean and despicable a Condition, yet I did not despise their Souls? Did I come to save them, and shall it be your work to destroy them?</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 How think ye? If a man have an hundred sheep, and one of them be gone astray? doth he not leave the ninety and nine, and goeth into the mountains, and seeketh that which is gone astray?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 And if so be that he find it, verily I say unto you, he rejoyceth more of that <ns0:hi>sheep,</ns0:hi> than of the ninety and nine which went not astray.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.<ns0:note place="bottom">We shall meet with the Parable, or Similitude more fully, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 15.4. To what purpose it is brought here, our Lord hath told us, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. to shew us, <ns0:hi>That it is not the Will of our Heavenly Father, that the least and meanest Believer should perish.</ns0:hi> And every <ns0:hi>Scandal,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Offence</ns0:hi> (as I before shewed) hath a Tendency to destroy that Soul, before whom it is laid, or to which it is given. I take heed, saith our Savi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />our, of giving <ns0:hi>Scandals</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Offences</ns0:hi> to others, yea, tho you should have observed them in something slipping and going astray, you will be more uncharitable to Men, than you are to the Beasts which you keep, you do not thus with a Sheep, tho it be gone astray, you do not despise and neglect it, much less take Courses to drive it further. No, you rather leave the rest as being safe, and go, tho it be into the Mountains, to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cover the Sheep that is lost, and if you find it, have a greater Passion of joy for that one Sheep so covered, than for all the other. If you see some Error in any of my Sheep, if they do wander, should it not be your Care, rather to <ns0:hi>restore such in the Spirit of Meekness</ns0:hi>? as <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.1. than to lay further Stumbling-Blocks before them, and give them occasion of fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:hi>Stumbling</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Falling</ns0:hi>? My Father hath done so for lost Man, my coming to seek and to save that which is lost, is an Evidence to you, that it is not his Will, that one of my little ones should be lost.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Moreover if thy brother shall trespass a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst thee, go and tell him his fault, betwixt thee, and him alone: If he shall hear thee, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jam. 5.20.</ns0:note> thou hast gained thy brother.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 But if he will not hear <ns0:hi>thee, then</ns0:hi> take with thee one or two more, that in <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 8.1. 2 Cor. 13.17.1. Heb. 10.28.</ns0:note> the mouth of two or three witnesses, every word may be establish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it to the church, but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be to thee as an <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 16, 17. 2 Thes. 3.14. 2 Joh. 10.</ns0:note> heathen man, and a publican.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviour very appositely addeth this, to his former Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course concerning <ns0:hi>avoiding Offences.</ns0:hi> That none might think, that by the former Doctrine he had made void the Law, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 19.17. which commanded all <ns0:hi>in any wise to rebuke their Neighbour, and not to suffer sin upon him,</ns0:hi> pretending that it was their Duty in some Cases to offend any Person by that Law. He here telleth them that he would not be so understood, as if they might not tell Offenders of their sins for fear of offending them, this had been to have with held Charity from their Souls under a pretence of <ns0:hi>Charity.</ns0:hi> Only in these Reproofs we must keep an Order, which Order he here prescribes. 1. Doing it <ns0:hi>privately, betwixt them, and him alone.</ns0:hi> 2. If that had not its Effect, <ns0:hi>then taking two or three with them.</ns0:hi> 3. If that also proved ine<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ectual, then <ns0:hi>telling it to the Church.</ns0:hi> 4. If thy Brother trespass against thee.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>Brother,</ns0:hi> here he meaneth any Christian, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.12. In such Cases it is the Will of God, not that we should Blazon and Publish them, but being certain that any Christian hath so offended, it is our Duty first <ns0:hi>to go to him, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t heard in matter of Fact, that he hath spoken or done, b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t shew him also the Sinfulness of it. <ns0:hi>If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy Brother</ns0:hi>: That is, if he Confesseth the sin<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and be brought to a sight of it, a sorrow for it, and a Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solution against it for the time to come, thou hast gained the Soul of thy Brother. <ns0:hi>But if he will not hear thee.</ns0:hi> If he either denieth the matter of Fact, that he did such a thing, or (admitting that) standeth to justifie the Fact, as what he might do: Then <ns0:hi>take with thee one or two more, that in the Mouth of two or three Witnesses, every word may be Established.</ns0:hi> One or two more, either such, as may be of more Authority with him, whose Words may probably be of more weight than thine with him, or who may witness the matter of Fact if it be denied, or at least witness by Chari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />table Admonition of him, and his Contumacy, if he refuseth to hearken to thee, and to repent, and reform. What was the Law of God, in civil and judicial Causes <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 19.15. God would have observed in Ecclesiastical Causes. <ns0:hi>One Witness shall not rise up against a Man for any iniquity, nor for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth; at the Mouth of two Witnesses, or at the Mouth of three Witnesses, shall the matter be Esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blished.</ns0:hi> And so the words in <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> should be translated, or at least understood. <ns0:hi>Every Word,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>every Matter</ns0:hi> be confirmed. <ns0:hi>And if he should neglect to hear them.</ns0:hi> Either, refuse to speak with them, or to suffer them to speak with him, or hearing them with his Ears, if he persists to deny the Fact, or to justifie the Fact, as if it were no sin, or go on still in the same Course (all these things are to be under<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ood by the term of <ns0:hi>not Hearing) If he shall not hear them, tell it to the Church.</ns0:hi> That the term <ns0:hi>Church</ns0:hi> is a Noun of mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titude, is Evident, and therefore cannot be under<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ood of any particular Person. Some would by the Church here under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand the <ns0:hi>Political Magistrate,</ns0:hi> but as this Sense is imbraced by very few, so it is very improbable, that our Saviour should send Christians in that Age to the Civil Magistrates, when they were all great Haters, and Persecuters of the Christian Religion, especially in Cases that were not punishable by the Judges, for no deliberate Person will say, that the <ns0:hi>Offences</ns0:hi> mentioned in this Text, were all of that Nature, as a Civil Judicature might take notice of them. Others say, that by the <ns0:hi>Church</ns0:hi> is here meant, the <ns0:hi>Iewish Court</ns0:hi> called the <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim,</ns0:hi> which had a mixed Cognizance, both of Civil and <ns0:hi>Ecclesi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />astical Causes.</ns0:hi> There are three Prejudices against this. 1. That the <ns0:hi>Iewish Court,</ns0:hi> was never in Scripture called <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. 2. That it is not probable, that our Saviour would direct Christians to go to the <ns0:hi>Iewish Courts</ns0:hi> in such Cases. 3. That the <ns0:hi>Sanhedrim</ns0:hi> was too great a Court to be troubled with all Scandals, tho they did take Cognizance of some things in Religion, which were of a grand concern. Such as <ns0:hi>Blasphe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />my, Idolatry, False Prophets,</ns0:hi> &c Others therefore under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand it of the <ns0:hi>Christian Church</ns0:hi>: Against this Opinion, there is this great <ns0:hi>Prejudice,</ns0:hi> that there was no such thing in being at that time; but I take this to be a lighter Objection than those, against the two other Opinions. 1. Because we need not understand our Saviour, speaking with Relation to the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent time, but the time to come, and giving Laws which should take place, and abide from the gathering of the Chri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stian Church, to the end of the World. Nor is it necessary, that we should take the term <ns0:hi>Church</ns0:hi> hrere in the strict Sense, in which it is most generally used in the Scriptures of the <ns0:hi>New Testament,</ns0:hi> for the general Notion of the Word, is only a <ns0:hi>Company of People</ns0:hi> called together, and in this Sense, <ns0:hi>Tell the Church,</ns0:hi> is no more than tell the <ns0:hi>Multitude,</ns0:hi> make his Crime more publick: Now what that multitude was which our Saviour meant, would easily be understood, when the Churches came to be formed. But the next Verse will make it more plain, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18. <ns0:hi>Verily I say unto you, wha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>soever you shall bind on Earth, shall be bound in Heaven,</ns0:hi> &c. By the <ns0:hi>Church,</ns0:hi> then must be meant, those who had Power to <ns0:hi>Bind,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Loose.</ns0:hi> Now tho, at this time, there was no particular Church formed, yet there were some who had a Power to <ns0:hi>Bind,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Loose,</ns0:hi> Christ had given such a Power to his <ns0:hi>Ap<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>stles.</ns0:hi> These were the present Church, and at this time in being. They were afterwards to constitute particular Churches, to whom (when constituted) in force of this Precept, such Offences were to be told. There are yet further Disputes, whether this Offence and Contumacy, be to be told only to the <ns0:hi>Rulers,</ns0:hi> or to the <ns0:hi>Multitude.</ns0:hi> I say to the <ns0:hi>whole Church,</ns0:hi> but first to the <ns0:hi>Rulers,</ns0:hi> then by them to the <ns0:hi>Multitude,</ns0:hi> not to Judge of it, but for their Consent, in casting a Person out of the Communion of the Church. Thus the <ns0:hi>incestuous Person</ns0:hi> was first accused to <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi>; then cast out by the Consent of the whole Church, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.3, 4. For it is unreasonable to think, that People should deny Communion to any, without knowing a justifiable Cause. And to no purpose, for<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Rulers in a Church to cast one out of its Communion, with whom the Members will have Communion. <ns0:hi>If he will not hear the Church, let him be unto thee as an Heathen and a Publican.</ns0:hi> That is, Esteem him as a <ns0:hi>Vile Person,</ns0:hi> for so they esteemed all <ns0:hi>Heathens,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Publicans.</ns0:hi> How far this could reach beyond having <ns0:hi>an Intimacy of Civil Communion with them,</ns0:hi> and a <ns0:hi>Communion with them in the Sacrament,</ns0:hi> I cannot understand, for as Christians were Licensed to a <ns0:hi>Civil</ns0:hi> Commerce with <ns0:hi>Heathens</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Publicans</ns0:hi>: So neither were <ns0:hi>Heathens,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Publicans,</ns0:hi> ever that we read of in Holy Writ, denyed the benefit of their Prayers, and hearing the Apostles preach. I am very well satisfyed, that the <ns0:hi>Primitive Church</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>id not deny to Persons Excommunicated, Liberty to be present at the <ns0:hi>Prayers of the Church,</ns0:hi> but it was long after the Apostles times, and whether grounded upon any Practice of their's, I much doubt. Christians had a Liberty to pray for any <ns0:hi>who had not sinned the sin unto Death.</ns0:hi> That they might not be present at such Prayers, I cannot learn from any thing in Holy Writ.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="18">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:252" />18 Verily I say unto you, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 20.23. 1 Cor. 5.4.</ns0:note> Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth, shall be bound in heaven, and whatso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever ye shall loose on earth, shall be loosed in heaven.<ns0:note place="bottom">We met with this Sentence, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 16. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19. where we observed that by <ns0:hi>Binding,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Loosing,</ns0:hi> was signified (according to the usage of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> of those times) <ns0:hi>declaring of Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />positions, true or false,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iudging things Lawful, or Vn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lawful.</ns0:hi> Some think that it hath no further import here; but it is the Opinion of Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvin,</ns0:hi> and other very judicious In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terpreters, that it is here to be extended to the <ns0:hi>Censures of the Church</ns0:hi>: The Sentence of the Church pronounced justly in the Case of Offences, and is added, lest Persons justly denied the Communion of the Church, should contemn such Censures. Chri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t assures these Persons, that such Censures ought not to be slighted<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for God would confirm them in Heaven, as also to their Absolutions, or Re-admissions of such Persons into their Communion, upon their true Repentance, an acknowledge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of their Errors. Not that our Lord by this intended to confirm all Sentences of <ns0:hi>Excommunication,</ns0:hi> or to patro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nize any Cheat or Hypocrisie in any, to gain an <ns0:hi>Absolution,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Restauration</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>Church.</ns0:hi> But only as to the first to assure stubborn, and impenitent Sinners, that he would ratifie what his Church did, according to the Rule he had given them to Act by. It is therefore a terrible Text, to those who are justly, and duly cut off from the Communion of the Church, for Notorious and Scandalous sins: Such as whoso committeth, and doth not repent of, they shall never enter into the King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom of God. And as Comfortable to those, who being so cast out do truly repent, and are under Temptations, to be swallowed up of too much Sorrow. If therefore any be cast out of any Church, for professing, or standing to any Truth of the Gospel, or because he will not do what is sinful; we must not understand them bound in Heaven, tho they be bound on Earth, nor have any such Excommunications any Terror in them. <ns0:hi>How forcible are right Words, but these arguings, what do they reprove?</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Church</ns0:hi> is not by this Text made infallible, nor is the Holy God, by it ingaged to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fend their Errors.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Again I say unto you, that if two of you shall agree on earth, as touching any thing that they shall ask, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Joh. 3.22. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 5.14.</ns0:note> it shall be done for them of my Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which is in heaven.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 For where two or three are gathered toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther in my name, there am I in the midst of them.<ns0:note place="bottom">Most Interpreters agree, a Connexion betwixt these Verses, and those immediately preceding, as if it were a further Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmation of what God had said concerning his <ns0:hi>Binding,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Loosing in Heaven,</ns0:hi> whatsoever they should <ns0:hi>Bind</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Loose on Earth,</ns0:hi> and say, the <ns0:hi>Asking</ns0:hi> mentioned in this Verse, sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poseth that no <ns0:hi>Church</ns0:hi> will adventure upon so Grave an Act as <ns0:hi>Excommunication,</ns0:hi> without asking his direction or Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel. Nor undertake such a thing as <ns0:hi>Absolution,</ns0:hi> without the like serious asking of God pardon for the repenting Sinner: Now saith he, Let the Church be never so small, that so joyn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth in Prayers on this occasion, what they ask of God shall be done. Whether it hath any such reference or no, or be an independent Promise of Christ's Presence with his Church, I shall not determine. Those who think this Text hath such a part<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>cular reference, yet do also grant it a more general Promise of Christ's Presence with his People. Whenever they are met by his Authority, or upon his Account or Command, whether it be for <ns0:hi>Counsel</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iudgment,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Prayer,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>the Ce<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lebration of any sacred Institution of his, he is in the midst of them,</ns0:hi> to Protect and Favour them: <ns0:hi>What they ask shall be done for them</ns0:hi> (that is, provided the thing ask<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed be good, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 7.11.) and for a right End, <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 4.3. and in a right manner, <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 18.1. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 1.5, 6, 7. Christ in this Text establisheth the Duty of Prayer in Communion with others. He doth not only require of his People <ns0:hi>secret Prayer, Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.6. but also praying in Company with others; the gathering together of his People for Prayer, whether in pri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vate Families, or more publick Congregations.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord! How often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Till seven times, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 6.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                     <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> hath something like this, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 17.4. but it seemeth to have been spoken at another time, and upon some other occasion, yet the Sense is much the same, and there are who think that <ns0:hi>Peters</ns0:hi> mention of seven times, arose from our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viours command there, that we should forgive our Brother, offending us seven times, when our Saviour by it intended not a certain and definite number, but a number incertain, and indefinite. But it is a greater Question, <ns0:hi>What sinning</ns0:hi>? And what <ns0:hi>Forgiveness</ns0:hi> is here meant? I cannot think that our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour here speaketh concerning the <ns0:hi>Churches absolving scan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dalous Sinners justly Excommunicated,</ns0:hi> but of the private Forgiveness of injuries done to us; it is not the Church, but I <ns0:hi>forgive him,</ns0:hi> for altho the Doors of the Church ought to be as open to a repenting Sinner, as the Doors of Heaven are, yet methinks both the Phrase of the Text, and the following Parable (which seemeth to me a Comment upon this Text) seems to lead us to the Interpretation of these Verses, as to private <ns0:hi>Wrongs</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Injuries,</ns0:hi> they are properly <ns0:hi>sins against us,</ns0:hi> and such as it is in every single Persons power to forgive. But it seems hard, that Christians should be obliged to forgive another his private Wrongs, so often as he doth them, if he will go on without end, multiplying Affronts and Injuries to us; we must therefore know, that our Saviour by this Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept doth not oblige any to take his Enemy into his Bosom, and make him his intimate, or Confident again; but only to lay aside all <ns0:hi>Malice,</ns0:hi> all <ns0:hi>Thoughts</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Desires of Revenge</ns0:hi> to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards him, to put on a Charitable frame of Spirit towards him, so as to be ready to do him any common Offices of Friendship: Thus far we are obliged to forgive those that do us Injuries, so often as they stand in need of Forgiveness; the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3.8. speaks of Wrath, Malice, &c. as pieces of the Old man, which every true Christian hath put off, and calls upon us, in <ns0:hi>Malice</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>be Children.</ns0:hi>

                     </ns0:gap> 2.13.</ns0:note> So likewise shall my heavenly Father, do also unto you, if ye from your hearts, forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.<ns0:note place="bottom">All these Verses (except the last) are but a <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> which (as I before shewed) Is a Similitude brought from the usual Actions of Men, and made use of to open, or apply some spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual Doctrine. The main Scope, or the Proposition of Truth, which our Saviour designes to open, or Press in that which is first and Principally to be considered, and intended, that as I before shewed, is to be known, either, by the particular Explication given by our Saviour, or by what went immedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ately before, or followeth immediately after. The Scope of this Parable is plainly exprest, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. <ns0:hi>So also shall my Heaven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly Father do unto you, if you from your Hearts, forgive not every one his Brother their Trespasses.</ns0:hi> Nor is it obscure<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly hinted to us, in what went before, where our Saviour was instructing <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> in the great Duty of <ns0:hi>forgiving Men their Trespasses:</ns0:hi> This being agreed, as we use to say, that <ns0:hi>Similitudes run not on four Feet,</ns0:hi> so we are not to expect, that all the Actions of Men mentioned in the Parable, should be answered by some Correspondent Actions of God, as Si<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />militudes always halt, so never more than when by them, Gods Actions are expressed, and represented to us. The main points which this Parable instructeth us in are. 1. <ns0:hi>That it is our Duty, especially theirs, who have received forgive<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness from God, to forgive their Brethren.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>That if they do not, they may justly question, whether God hath forgiven them, and expect the same Severity from him, which they shew unto their Brethren.</ns0:hi> These being the main things for instruction, in which, this Parable is brought, and which we ought chiefly to Eye, as the things taught us by this <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> nothing hindreth, but that it may also instruct us in some other things, tho we cannot raise a Proposition of Truth, from every Branch of the <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> and some things be put in according to the Passions, and usual dealings of Men, which possibly are in them <ns0:hi>unrighteous Actions,</ns0:hi> and may follow from their ungoverned Passions, which will by no means agree to the pure, and Holy Nature of God. I will first open such terms in the Parable, as may be less in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tellegible to Vulgar Readers. <ns0:hi>The Kingdom of Heaven.</ns0:hi> My Administration of my Kingdom: I am come to purchase Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mission of sins, and to dispense out <ns0:hi>Remission of sins,</ns0:hi> to those who are indebted to the Justice of my Father, but in the Application of my Blood, to Men and Women, for the Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mission of their sins, both <ns0:hi>my Father</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> self, will do as a <ns0:hi>King, that took Account of his Servants,</ns0:hi> &c. Men must look for Pardon from my Father, and benefit from me as their Redeemer, upon the following terms. <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 6.15. [<ns0:hi>ten Thousand Talents</ns0:hi>] a certain, for an incertain Number, a very great Sum. Those who have computed it, say it amounteth to a <ns0:hi>Million,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Eight Hundred, seventy five Thousand Pounds. [He commanded him to be sold, and his Wife and Children, and all he had.</ns0:hi>) A thing which our Law will not suffer, but in use amongst other Nations, and amongst the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> in particular, as may be learned from, 2 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 4.1. [and <ns0:hi>he delivered him to the Tormentors</ns0:hi>] that is, to the Keepers of the Prison, so the next Words teach us, and the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Word often signifieth no more, tho it doth indeed sometimes; <ns0:hi>An Hundred Pence, v.</ns0:hi> 28. signifieth a small Sum, hardly exceeding in our Mony <ns0:hi>Fifty shillings.</ns0:hi> This Parable, excellently instructeth us in these Truths. 1. That as Men by the Law of Nature, and God, and the Laws of Men, may be Debtors to us, to our <ns0:hi>Reputation,</ns0:hi> to our <ns0:hi>Estate.</ns0:hi> So we are all Debtors, to the Glory, Honour, and Justice of God. 2. That it is a vast Debt we owe to Gods Honour and Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stice; to which no Debt owning by any to us, can bear any Proportion. 3. That we have nothing to pay to God, in Satis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />faction for our Debt. 4. That God hath a right to demand a full Satisfaction of us. 5. That God for Christ's sake, upon our Applications to him for Mercy will forgive us our Debts. 6. That we are not so ready to forgive our Brethren their little Injuries, as God is to forgive us. 7. That our Diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culty to forgive our Brethren, after Gods Liberality in forgiving us, is a great Charge, or will be a great Charge against us, in the Court of Heaven. 8. That we ought to set before us Gods Compassion towards us, and free Love in forgiving us, potently to move us, to forgive those who have done us Injury, and to forgive them out of that Consideration. 9.                      </ns0:gap>raits, are in our Power. 10. That the not doing of this, will be an ill Evidence to our Souls: That God hath not indeed forgiven us, as well as a Bar against such forgivness, and an ill <ns0:hi>Omen,</ns0:hi> that some Punishment from God expecteth us in this Life, to bring us to a Temper more Conformable to the Gospel, and if not, in this Life, yet in the Life which is to come.</ns0:note>
